1. The animation shows a historical comparison of buying versus renting across US housing markets. Each house on a street stands for a purchase date. A lit house means the buyer was ahead after ten years. A dark house means the renter was ahead. The frames single out one house, "The darkest house," for June 2006. Buying then left the buyer $82,385 behind a renter. The data sources are FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac rates. The chart is labeled "ILLUSTRATIVE" and "US only · history, not a forecast."

2. Very little changes across the six frames. The title "The darkest house" in frames 1–2 is replaced by the "$82,385 behind" figure from frame 3 onward. The June 2006 house stays the same, and the surrounding street barely shifts. The frames look like the start of a reveal: first the label, then the dollar result.

3. It means that timing mattered a lot. Someone who bought at the 2006 price peak, just before the housing crash, was worse off after ten years than if they had rented. This is the worst case on the street. Most of the other houses are lit, so buying usually came out ahead over ten years, and the dark houses are the exception.

4. A viewer could take away that the purchase date and price level affect whether buying beats renting, and that buying is not guaranteed to win. The only caution printed on screen is "history, not a forecast," and it points the other way from any prediction. The frames give no instruction to buy or to rent.

5. The animation did not suggest any advice. The picture and text only show the 2006 outcome and the "history, not a forecast" caveat. The takeaway about timing risk in 4 is my own conclusion. For your own question, these frames don't say whether renting costs more than buying today. They show only one historical worst case.
